title: The Starlight Club
clue: A club that meets after dark, with a blanket for a clubhouse and the brightest guest in the sky.
reveal: On a clear evening, settle outside with your dog and look for the Dog Star, Sirius, the brightest star in the night sky. The club closes when your dog decides it is time to go in.
objective: Spend a calm evening in your own yard, balcony or doorstep with your dog, find the Dog Star and invent a constellation named after your dog.
instructions: Pick a clear, mild evening and a private spot with no steps: your yard, balcony or doorstep. Check sunset time. Sirius shows in the evening sky in winter in the northern hemisphere, so look low in the southeast or south after dark.
Take your dog's favorite blanket (the Club Blanket), warm layers for you, a dim clip-on light for your dog's collar, and a leash. If you like, use a free star-map app with the screen dimmed.
Open the club: lay the Club Blanket and let your dog settle, sniff, watch or wander the leash length. Whichever spot they choose on or beside it is the club president's chair. Nothing is required.
Find Orion first: three bright stars in a short row make his belt. Follow the line downward to the very brightest star. That is Sirius, in the constellation of the Great Dog.
Say hello to Sirius once in a quiet voice, then give your dog a slow shoulder rub or their favorite toy as the club toast. Go quiet for a minute and listen with your dog: what do they notice?
If clouds spoil it, pick any bright star, planet or light and call it your Dog Star for the night.
Invent your own constellation: choose three or four stars, join them in your mind and name them for your dog.
When your dog is ready to go in, the club is adjourned. At home, draw your constellation with a white pencil or crayon on dark paper.
twist: Your dog is club president and the club adjourns when they say so. The aim is the Dog Star, and the prize is a constellation you name for them.
variations: Out of season: Sirius rises late in summer, so pick the brightest star or planet instead, or look for the Moon.
Seated version: stay on a chair by your door, or watch from a window with the lights off.
Cold-night version: keep it to ten minutes with a coat or blanket for you both, and go in at the first shiver.
Quiet version: skip the app and the drawing and just watch the sky together.
completion: You have spent your club meeting outside with your dog, looked for the Dog Star, and adjourned when they were ready.
photoIdea: Your dog on the blanket against the evening sky, taken from behind or the side with low light.
memoryPrompt: What did you name your dog's constellation, and how did they spend the club meeting?
supplies: A dim clip-on light for the collar
optionalSupplies: Dark paper and white pencil or crayon
substitutes: A towel or coat instead of a blanket
A reflective collar instead of a clip-on light
safety: Keep your dog leashed or in a closed yard in the dark, with ID on and a light so you can see them.
Choose a mild night; use a blanket, and go in if your dog shivers or wants to leave.
Skip nights with fireworks or loud noise, and never leave your dog outside alone.
